priority_fields.value: The glass transition of a material occurs across a range of temperatures but is often described by a single representative glass transition temperature, Tg. If using Dynamic Mechanical Analysis (DMA), Tg can be defined as the peak of Loss Modulus or peak Tan Delta, which are relatively straightforward to compute. One can also use Storage Modulus data to define an onset Tg, which is based on the intersection of a tangent line at the inflection point in the E' curve with a horizontal line at the "glassy plateau" region. This interactive Vega-Lite plot shows how to compute the derivative and approximate the onset Tg using various window and aggregation transforms. Hover over a data series in the bottom plot to reveal the intersecting lines and approximated onset Tg. These DMA data series were curated from Hoepfner et al. (2018, doi: 10.1002/app.46157). For further comparisons of the various methodologies for computing Tg, see https://www.tainstruments.com/pdf/literature/RH100.pdf.
Calculating Onset Tg with the Derivative of Storage Modulus vs. Temperature

priority_fields.value: This interactive Vega-Lite chart compares the properties of polymer nanocomposite samples with the processing steps used to create those samples. Hover over a point or bar to display a tooltip with additional information. The width of each bar in the Gantt chart on the right signifies the duration of a given process step, and the color of the bar corresponds to the text description linked to the step. These data were curated from Liao et al. (2004, doi: 10.1016/j.msea.2004.06.031), and they help to convey the degree to which the processing of a material can impact its measurable attributes such as glass transition temperature, Tg. Use the mouse to pan or zoom in either plot.

priority_fields.value: A Gantt chart can be a useful tool for displaying temporal information that spans ranges, such as a sequence of processes. In this example, we query curated processing steps for a nanocomposite sample involving a reported time interval and display as ranged bar marks colored by the type of sub-process. Because the units of time vary, values are converted into minutes using Vega-Lite's calculate transform. The window transform is used for computing the cumulative duration, which assumes that the process steps occur immediately after one another and in a serial fashion. In this case, the steps get progressively longer in duration, so a symlog scale is used along the x-axis (Gantt charts almost always use a linear scale). Hover over a bar to view a tooltip with the actual duration. These data were curated from Goertzen et al. (2007, doi: 10.1016/j.compositesa.2008.02.006).

priority_fields.value: Oftentimes, optimizing a material involves weighing among tradeoffs, such as mechanical stiffness versus ductility. This Vega-Lite chart shows one way to compare more than one property along the vertical axis using a layered plot with points connected by rule marks. One way to use this plot would be to define the quadrant or region of interest (e.g. high-strength, high-stiffness, high-ductility) and compare existing materials samples with the target. These data have been curated from Ye et al. (2006, DOI: 10.1002/pola.21650).

priority_fields.value: Whether you are trying to optimize a single material property or combination of properties, sometimes a visualization can help compare the top result against viable alternatives. This series of plots compares polymer nanocomposite samples whose temperature-dependent thermal conductivity, as well as electrical conductivity, have been curated into MaterialsMine. The green regions represent samples with a combination of high electrical conductivity and low thermal conductivity. This chart also makes use of joinaggregate transforms to calculate means and quartile boundaries for the error bars. These example data were curated from Chandrasekaran et al. (2013, doi: 10.1016/j.eurpolymj.2013.10.008).

priority_fields.value: Materials undergoing deformation can exhibit a combination of elastic and viscous behavior. Under static loads, viscoelastic behavior can manifest as stress relaxation or strain creep behavior. Another way to quantify material viscoelasticity is under dynamic loading conditions, for example in rheometry and dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA). For example, in DMA, a sinusoidal stress is applied and the strain response is measured. The in-phase component (storage modulus) and out-of-phase component (loss modulus) are related by the phase shift (delta), each of which can be influenced by temperature or strain rate. In this chart, temperature and frequency sweep data come from Stoeckelhuber et al. (Macromolecules 2011, DOI: 10.1021/ma1026077).

priority_fields.value: This example build upon an example developed for binary material combinations. The UpSet plot is a novel technique developed by Lex et al. (2014, DOI: 10.1109/TVCG.2014.2346248) for visualizing set intersections as a matrix layout. A sorted bar chart along the top shows the number of intersections of the sets (shown as connected dots) in the matrix below. Along the left hand side, a bar chart shows the size of each set. This chart shows the largest ternary intersections of material components in the knowledge graph, where the size of each intersection corresponds to the number of nanocomposite samples with that combination of material components. The plot was achieved in Vega-Lite through the use of the joinaggregate, calculate, window, and filter transforms as well as concatenated and layered views. Hover over data marks to view tooltips.

priority_fields.value: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measures the amount of heat energy put into (or removed from) a system in order to maintain a pre-defined heating or cooling profile. When a phase transition occurs, a change in the heat flow is observed. To compute the glass transition temperature, Tg, from DSC data, you can identify the inflection point in the heat flow curves by taking the derivative and looking for the minimum. This Vega-Lite shows how to compute such a derivative within the chart specification, and the reported values of Tg are overlaid as rule and text marks on the lower plot. As you can see, the results match quite nicely! These example DSC curves have been curated from Ash et al. (2004, doi: 10.1002/polb.20297).

priority_fields.value: Stress-strain data from tensile tests are plotted for samples from the published work of Gao et al. (2012, Polymers, DOI: 10.3390/polym4010187), which studied DGEBA epoxy resin nanocomposites with silicon dioxide nanoparticles as a filler. The reported tensile modulus values (units of GPa) are displayed upon highlighting a given sample's stress-strain curve. Since the tensile modulus is determined by the slope of the linear elastic region of a stress-strain plot, a line segment with a slope corresponding to the tensile modulus is also displayed.

priority_fields.value: Getting its name from an 1979 album cover by rock band Joy Division, a "Joy Plot" (also known as a "Ridgeline Plot") shows multiple data series aligned along the horizontal axis and offset with slight overlap along the vertical axis. This interactive Vega-Lite version of a joy plot with MaterialsMine data displays representative Tan Delta versus Temperature curves from dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) experiments. Hover over a data series to display the reported glass transition temperature, Tg, and standard deviation (solid line and colored band) as well as the computed Tg of the representative curve (dashed line) based on the peak position of Tan Delta. Data were curated from Ramanathan et al. (2012, doi: 10.1002/polb.23037).
